questions.q: What is the output of `typeof null` in JavaScript, and why does this result often surprise beginners who expect it to be `"null"`?
questions.a: The output is `"object"`. This is a long-standing JavaScript quirk from the first implementation where `null` was represented as a null pointer (0x00) which the `typeof` operator identified as an object. Beginners expect `"null"` because `null` is a primitive value, but `typeof` returns `"object"` for `null`. A wrong answer (e.g., `"null"` or `"undefined"`) reveals the student has memorised the primitive list but hasn't encountered this specific historical bug that appears in CBSE theory questions and competitive exam MCQs.

questions.q: Explain the difference between `let` and `const` in terms of reassignment and mutation. If you declare `const arr = [1, 2];`, can you execute `arr.push(3)`? Can you execute `arr = [4, 5];`? Justify both answers.
questions.a: `let` allows reassignment (binding a new value to the same variable name); `const` forbids reassignment but allows mutation of the object/array it references. `arr.push(3)` works because it mutates the existing array object — the binding `arr` still points to the same array. `arr = [4, 5]` fails with `TypeError: Assignment to constant variable` because it attempts to rebind `arr` to a new array. A student who says both fail or both work confuses reassignment with mutation — a critical distinction for CBSE practicals where `const` is preferred for arrays/objects that will be modified in place.

questions.q:
Predict the output of each expression and explain the type coercion rule applied:
(a) `"10" + 5`
(b) `"10" - 5`
(c) `true + 2`
(d) `null + 1`
(e) `undefined + 1`
questions.a: (a) `"105"` — `+` with a string operand triggers string concatenation; number 5 is coerced to `"5"`. (b) `5` — `-` is not defined for strings, so both operands are coerced to numbers (`10 - 5`). (c) `3` — `true` coerces to `1` in numeric context. (d) `1` — `null` coerces to `0` in numeric context. (e) `NaN` — `undefined` coerces to `NaN` in numeric context; any arithmetic with `NaN` yields `NaN`. A student answering `"105"`, `"5"`, `"true2"`, `"null1"`, `"undefined1"` treats all operators as string concatenation, missing that only `+` performs concatenation — a classic CBSE board trap.

questions.q:
Compare `==` and `===` with these pairs. For each, state the result of both operators and explain WHY they differ or match:
(i) `0 == false` vs `0 === false`
(ii) `"" == false` vs `"" === false`
(iii) `null == undefined` vs `null === undefined`
(iv) `"5" == 5` vs `"5" === 5`
questions.a: (i) `0 == false` → `true` (both coerce to 0); `0 === false` → `false` (number vs boolean, different types). (ii) `"" == false` → `true` (both coerce to 0); `"" === false` → `false` (string vs boolean). (iii) `null == undefined` → `true` (special ECMA spec rule: they are loosely equal only to each other); `null === undefined` → `false` (different types: `object` vs `undefined`). (iv) `"5" == 5` → `true` (string coerced to number); `"5" === 5` → `false` (string vs number). A student claiming `===` is "stricter `==`" without explaining the coercion steps misses the mechanistic difference — CBSE asks "why" in 2-mark questions.

What is JavaScript variables? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: JavaScript variables are named containers for storing data values that can be changed during program execution, declared using var, let, or const keywords with let and const being block-scoped (ES6+).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: JavaScript variables are named containers for storing data values that can be changed during program execution, declared using var, let, or const keywords with let and const being block-scoped (ES______+).
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about JavaScript variables?
questions.a: Students believe const makes the value immutable (like final in Java).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can declare variables using appropriate keywords (let/const), identify and explain the 7 primitive types and object type, predict the output of expressions involving type coercion (e.g., "5" + 3 vs "5" - 3), correctly choose between == and === in conditional logic, and write a 5-line script that reads two numbers from prompt.
